chunks.text: SPH3U B2.1 covers terminology used to describe motion.
SPH3U B2.2 concerns interpreting graphs relating position, velocity, acceleration and time in one dimension.
SPH3U B3.1 addresses average, instantaneous and constant speed, velocity and acceleration.
SPH3U C3.3 applies Newton’s laws to qualitative explanations of forces.

chunks.text: Average velocity is displacement divided by elapsed time: v_avg = Δx/Δt. Displacement has direction. Speed is scalar and average speed is total distance divided by elapsed time. Returning to a starting point can give zero average velocity while distance and average speed are positive. Use metres and seconds for m/s. Example: displacement +20 m over 4 s gives +5 m/s. An instant requires a local rate, not a finite-interval average.

Average acceleration is change in velocity divided by elapsed time: a_avg = (v_final − v_initial)/Δt. Units are m/s². Example: velocity rises from +2 m/s to +8 m/s in 3 s, giving +2 m/s². Negative acceleration does not always mean slowing down; compare its direction with velocity. A negative velocity and negative acceleration increase speed. Time must be positive for these examples.

For constant acceleration in one dimension, x(t)=x0+v0*t+0.5*a*t² and v(t)=v0+a*t. The slope of position-time gives velocity; slope of velocity-time gives acceleration. Signed area under velocity-time gives displacement, not generally total distance. These equations assume constant acceleration throughout the interval. For x0=0 m, v0=2 m/s, a=3 m/s² and t=4 s, position is 32 m and velocity is 14 m/s.

In an inertial frame with constant mass, net force F_net=m*a. Net force is the vector sum of forces, not necessarily one applied force. If m=2 kg and a=3 m/s², F_net=6 N. With zero net force, an object can move at constant nonzero velocity. Action-reaction forces act on different objects; they do not cancel in one object’s force sum.

For uniform circular motion, speed is constant while the direction of velocity changes. Velocity is tangent; centripetal acceleration points to the centre with magnitude a=v²/r, r>0. With v=6 m/s and r=3 m, a=12 m/s² inward. Angular speed ω=v/r in rad/s. Tangential acceleration a_t=r*α for fixed radius; a_t is distinct from inward acceleration. An object may have α=0 yet nonzero centripetal acceleration. This is enrichment; no SPH3U expectation mapping is asserted.

Convert quantities to compatible units before substituting: 100 cm=1 m, 1000 m=1 km, 60 s=1 min, 1000 g=1 kg. Divide km/h by 3.6 to get m/s. Dimensions of acceleration are length/time² and of force mass*length/time². Displayed examples use six significant digits; numerical grading allows 0.5% relative error or 1e-8 absolute error. This tolerance is a prototype choice, not an official marking rule.
